title: Displaying Math Fonts in Compose Text

message.title: You · 18 Sep
message.text: Hi Matt, is 1729 an interesting number or a boring number?

message.title: Matt (Math) · Pack: Sample
message.text:
Hi! 1729 is actually quite an interesting number. It's famously known as the Hardy-Ramanujan number. The story goes that the mathematician G.H. Hardy visited Srinivasa Ramanujan in the hospital and mentioned that the taxi he had taken had the number 1729, which he thought was a dull one. Ramanujan immediately replied that it was, in fact, a very interesting number because it is the smallest number that can be expressed as the sum of two cubes in two different ways:

\[1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3\]

This property makes 1729 a unique and fascinating number in the realm of mathematics!

message.text: Hmmm... how does that compare to simply using some kind of rich text modifier

message.title: Matt (Math) · Pack: Sample
message.text: Using a rich text modifier can certainly simplify the process of displaying mathematical fonts in a Compose Text Element in Kotlin. Rich text modifiers allow you to apply different styles and formatting to different parts of your text, including mathematical symbols and equations. This can be especially useful if you want to display complex mathematical expressions or if you want to highlight certain parts of your text. However, it's important to note that rich text modifiers may not always provide the same level of control and customization as using `SpanStyle` or other more advanced text styling techniques. Ultimately, the best approach will depend on your specific needs and preferences.
